items.title: America is running out of skilled workers. Carhartt’s CEO has a ‘radical’ idea to fix it
items.summary:
Good morning!

Carhartt CEO Linda Hubbard is proposing an idea she concedes may be “a bit radical” to solve the skilled trades shortage: pay people to learn the jobs employers desperately need to fill.

“I think if companies truly need these workers, then they have to put some money behind it,” Hubbard told me at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit last week.

Employers will need to fill roughly 1.7 million skilled trades openings every year through 2035, according to a report from the Alliance for America’s Skilled Trades. Compounding the problem is that nearly a quarter of skilled tradespeople are over 55 and nearing retirement.

Hubbard wants more companies to embrace an “earn while you learn” model. She pointed to Henry Ford College in Michigan, where students in a two-year auto technician program alternate between eight weeks in the classroom and eight weeks at a dealership. They emerge with a certificate and a well-paying job, Hubbard said. Building that bridge from classroom to career “is how you’re going to get that high retention rate,” she said.

Google and the nonprofit Jobs for the Future are testing a related approach. Last year, they partnered to offer apprentices up to $2,000 to offset childcare, transportation, and housing costs—some of the biggest barriers for those interested in the skilled trades, said Maria Flynn, CEO of Jobs for the Future.

The payments are designed to plug what Flynn calls leaks in the apprenticeship pipeline. Fewer than half of apprentices complete their programs, and only 29 of every 100 who start are still working in a…
items.t: America is running out of skilled workers. Carhartt’s CEO has a ‘radical’ idea to fix it

items.title: AI is moving fast. Can companies keep up?
items.summary:
Good morning. AI’s most consequential business story may be less about the arrival of superintelligence than about whether companies can keep pace.

A new feature article by Fortune’s AI editor Jeremy Kahn explores the concept of “the Singularity”—a hypothesized turning point when AI drives technological change faster than humans can keep up. Patrick and John Collison, cofounders of payments company Stripe, wrote a letter to investors in August announcing that as of Jan. 1, the world had entered this dynamic, “and we have since been operating on that basis.”

“For Stripe, the Singularity’s economic harbingers came in the form of a surge of new business creation and an acceleration of those companies’ growth,” Kahn writes. Stripe told Fortune that beginning in January, it had seen unusual and sustained spikes in many of the metrics it tracks. For example, new customer sign-ups rose 50% year over year, the biggest jump ever, while the median business in its 2026 cohort of new customers generated 50% more revenue than the median business in its 2025 cohort had at the same stage.

Those figures suggest a more dynamic startup economy, although they do not establish how much of the improvement AI caused. In the article, Kahn cites a recent McKinsey survey that found only about 37% of respondents reported that AI had contributed positively to their organizations’ earnings—and most reported gains were small. McKinsey discussed the findings in an August article .

Stripe is preparing for commerce in which AI agents initiate transactions on users’ behalf. “If the Singularity is…
items.t: AI is moving fast. Can companies keep up?

items.title: The jagged frontier gets a body
items.summary:
In August, at Beijing’s World Humanoid Robot Games, a robot called Tiangong Ultra ran 100 meters in 8.64 seconds , almost a second faster than Usain Bolt’s world record. A year earlier, at the Games’ first edition, the winning time had been 21.5 seconds . Yet this year’s champion could not stop: it crashed into the padded barrier beyond the finish line, along with several of its rivals. That is physical AI in a single race: breathtaking progress on some skills, persistent weakness on others. Knowing where that boundary lies, and how fast it is moving, is now a strategic question for every executive.

This fall, we spent a week in Shenzhen and Beijing visiting robotics companies, from start-ups founded by former Huawei and DJI engineers to firms that already ship robots by the tens of thousands. The founders we met cared less about sprint records than about one question: where can a robot be trusted to work today, and where can it not? Their answers convinced us of two things. Physical AI is the real AI revolution. And it is arriving far faster than companies or governments are preparing for.

The question has a familiar shape. In 2023, one of us was part of a team of researchers from Harvard Business School and other universities that ran a field experiment with 758 BCG consultants. On tasks within GPT-4’s reach, consultants using it finished 25% faster and produced work rated more than 40% higher in quality. On a task just beyond that reach, they were 19 percentage points less likely to reach the right answer. We called the boundary the jagged technological frontier :…
items.t: The jagged frontier gets a body

items.title: What does it take to overhaul a company bogged down by bureaucracy? Verizon’s transformation chief has 8,000 ideas
items.summary:
When Alfonso Villanueva proposed a new way to keep Verizon customers from leaving, he stumbled into a corporate obstacle course.

Villanueva, Verizon’s chief transformation officer, wanted to give wireless customers frustrated by high bills an incentive to stay. His idea: Let them add home internet service for just $10 or $15 a month, potentially saving them up to $60 on their combined household bills.

But when he asked how long it would take to roll out the offer, his team returned two days later with a presentation mapping out the process. It would require the involvement of more than 20 teams.

For Villanueva, who joined Verizon in November 2025 after previously working with CEO Dan Schulman at PayPal , the exercise laid bare the organizational complexity that had made his appointment necessary .

The number of teams involved in rolling out promotional offers has since dropped from more than 20 to three, while launch times for certain offers have shrunk from 10 days to just two hours.

That newfound speed is critical to Verizon’s efforts to regain ground lost to T-Mobile and AT&T. But streamlining promotional offers is just one piece of a much broader overhaul. Early in the transformation, Verizon asked employees to identify ways the company could improve, generating more than 8,000 suggestions. Villanueva used AI to help consolidate those ideas into broader priorities, building a program spanning hundreds of initiatives. Roughly 300 leaders have been enlisted to drive the changes alongside their regular responsibilities.

Villanueva’s bet is that individual…
items.t: What does it take to overhaul a company bogged down by bureaucracy? Verizon’s transformation chief has 8,000 ideas

items.title: Big AI doesn’t care about your data anymore. Now it’s stealing how you think
items.summary:
In 2004 I begged the people running America’s biggest media companies not to hand their ad inventory to Google for pennies on the dollar. Back then, I ran a company that sold pricing software, and the logo on the building changed with every meeting but the warning never did: if you crater your own prices, you’re teaching the market what you’re worth. Again and again the executives smiled politely and thanked me for my time.

They assumed I was just another entrepreneur selling my own book. And they assumed they’d be fine. Google was incremental revenue, and it would all work out.

It didn’t. American newspaper ad revenue went from $49 billion in 2005 to less than $10 billion in 2022 . Nearly 3,000 papers have closed, and two-thirds of the country’s newspaper journalists are gone . In 2025 a federal judge finally ruled that Google had illegally monopolized key parts of the ad-tech market those publishers depended on. By then the damage was done.

I had underestimated the danger. I thought the publishers were selling themselves too cheap. What they were actually selling was any reason for advertisers to need them in the first place. Google delivered ad infrastructure, gobbled up all the ads, learned who read what, and exactly what advertisers would pay to reach them. Soon advertisers could find the same readers anywhere on the web for a fraction of the price.

Two decades later, I’m sitting in similar rooms and I’m hearing “we’ll be fine” all over again.

The labs have engaged millions of people in the ultimate head fake: By highlighting the vast troves of data they use to…
items.t: Big AI doesn’t care about your data anymore. Now it’s stealing how you think

items.title: Current price of oil as of November 23, 2026
items.summary:
As of 7:45 a.m. Eastern Time today, oil sold for $92.05 per barrel (using Brent as the benchmark, which we’ll get into momentarily). That’s $76 cents lower than yesterday and approximately a $30 rise over the past year.

Oil price per barrel % Change Price of oil yesterday $92.81 -0.81% Price of oil 1 month ago $113.95 -19.21% Price of oil 1 year ago $62.34 +47.65% 

Will oil prices go up? 

It’s impossible to predict the future of oil prices. Several factors determine the movement of oil, but it ultimately boils down to supply and demand. Again, when threats of economic downturn, war, etc. are high, the oil trajectory can turn rapidly.

How oil prices translate to gas pump prices 

When you pay for gas at the pump, you’re paying for more than just the crude oil itself; you’re also springing for links along the chain, such as the refineries and wholesalers—not to mention taxes and local gas station markups.

Still, the crude oil aspect affects the final price most dramatically, as it typically accounts for more than half the price per gallon. When oil prices spike, so do gas prices. And frustratingly, when oil prices drop, gas prices tend to take their time drifting down to the lower price (sometimes referred to as “rockets and feathers”).

The role of the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve 

In case of emergency, the U.S. has a store of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its primary purpose is energy security in case of disaster (think sanctions, severe storm damage, even war). But it can also go a long way toward softening crippling price hikes during…

items.title: Payward and the coming wave of crypto consolidation
items.summary:
Eat or be eaten. That’s the choice facing crypto companies as they confront not just another market rout, but broader industry trends that are likely to wipe out numerous small players—and some larger ones—altogether. In this new landscape, the lines between banks, brokerages, and blockchains are getting blurred entirely, while scale matters more than ever. One firm that appears to have gotten the memo is Payward.

If you’re unfamiliar, Payward is the parent company of Kraken, one of the crypto industry’s oldest exchanges. Since March of 2025, the company has been on an epic M&A spree , acquiring 10 companies that include the stock trading platform NinjaTrader, crypto clearing house Bitnomial, and a bank in Lithuania. Last week, Payward capped all this by buying the VC firm and asset manager Tribe Capital, which has a reported $2.7 billion of AUM.

It’s not hard to see the strategy here. At a time when blockchain and Bitcoin have become just another part of the broader financial landscape, it’s hard for firms to succeed by simply slinging crypto assets and services. That’s why Payward is seeking to add everything from stock trading to full-blown banking .

In doing so, the company is positioning itself to acquire more customers, but also to escape the brutal feast-and-famine cycle that defines the traditional crypto industry—one where firms get fat on heavy trading during a bull run, and then hope those proceeds are enough to ride out the next crypto winter. By diversifying, Payward no longer has to live or die by these cycles. The Tribe acquisition , meanwhile, lays the…
items.t: Payward and the coming wave of crypto consolidation

items.title: Gen Z is choosing who sits at the Thanksgiving table, and it’s not always family
items.summary:
Thanksgiving has long reflected a familiar progression into American adulthood. Leave home, find a partner, purchase a home and eventually graduate from sitting at your parents’ table to hosting a holiday of your own.

Yet a 2025 U.S. Census Bureau report found that fewer than one-quarter of 25- to 34-year-old Americans had reached the four conventional milestones of adulthood—moving out, working, marrying and having children—compared with nearly half in 1975. Marriage and parenthood are happening later, homeownership is financially challenging, and more young people are building lives outside the nuclear-family household.

So, what does the American Dream look like for the next generation when a flex wall is more commonplace than a white picket fence?

Thanksgiving offers a window into how young people are adapting, from changing relationships and family structures to a more globalized youth culture. Brands still building strategies around traditional milestones risk overlooking emerging consumer needs and entirely new occasions for growth.

The Thanksgiving table is changing because the people around it are changing.

Friendsgiving predates Gen Z, but it has become an established part of young adults’ holiday calendars. New research conducted by Ogilvy and Ideally, a nationally representative survey of 1,198 U.S. adults fielded Nov. 11–12, found that 41% of Gen Z consider Friendsgiving equally or more meaningful than Thanksgiving with family or relatives. And Gen Zers are almost twice as likely as the general population to choose Friendsgiving outright as their most…
items.t: Gen Z is choosing who sits at the Thanksgiving table, and it’s not always family

Mississippi hadn’t sent a new Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1947. Then Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, asked about high beef prices, said Mississippians have “so many proteins to choose from.”

Her opponent, Scott Colom, turned it into a 28-second ad: “Pick another protein? Sheee-it, I’d rather pick another senator instead,” an Army veteran says in it. Colom won. 

Democrats also took a Senate seat and the governor’s mansion in Texas, where James Talarico beat Ken Paxton and Gina Hinojosa unseated Gov. Greg Abbott. In Alaska, Mary Peltola’s win over Sen. Dan Sullivan, called Nov. 17, gave Democrats a 56-44 Senate majority. Peltola ran on Alaskans’ frustration with high fuel prices and other costs.

Voters were angry about “affordability” during the off-year elections of 2025 that, among other things, crowned Zohran Mamdani as one of America’s most popular politicians. Then they spent the year being told to adjust. If beef is too expensive, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said, “you can eat chicken, pork, salmon, eggs.” A Chevron executive, Andy Walz, said in April people should drive less as the Iran war pushed up gas prices. President Donald Trump called the price at the pump “a small price to pay.”

Heather Long has the data on what all that adjusting looks like. The chief economist for the Navy Federal Credit Union and a former Washington Post economics columnist, her father was an Army veteran, and she was a member of the credit union “many years before I ever thought of working here,” she told Fortune . She spent years writing about the K-shaped economy, the rich…
items.t: Top economist on the ‘psychological tax’ you pay at the grocery store: It’s ‘on steroids’ compared with the Great Recession

items.title: A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue | John Harris
items.summary:
Last week’s Milburn review contained telling phrases, but the core problem is not Neets: it’s what capitalism as we know it has done to employment

Everyday pride and contentment. That’s what work should give us. In 15-plus years of speaking to ordinary people and politicians about the UK’s serial woes and crises, one thing has revealed itself to me time and time again: the mess of cant, contradictions and tensions in our national understanding of work. Indeed, the higher up the hierarchies of power and influence any conversation about work goes, the more one vitally important subject seems to fall away: what paid employment actually is or ought to be.

All of this is reflective of a very British kind of amnesia. Of course poorly rewarded, unreliable jobs have always been part of our economy – and in the past a focus of fierce social conflict. But well within living memory a combination of the power of trade unions and the collective social conscience built into the postwar consensus resulted in an economy and labour market that now seem almost inconceivable. For sure they were scattered with restrictive practices and base prejudice: fathers securing jobs for their sons, people from minorities being excluded from work not just by people in management but by their fellow workers, and a great deal of…

items.title: ‘Folks are struggling in many cases’: GoFundMe’s CEO says affordability crisis is behind 40% surge in U.S. fundraisers for essentials like groceries
items.summary:
As more Americans struggle to put food on the table, crowdsourcing money for groceries has become consumers’ balm to an ongoing affordability crisis.

Food-related GoFundMe fundraisers have increased 35% year-over-year in the platform’s English-speaking markets of the U.S., Canada, UK, Australia, and Ireland, including a 40% jump in the U.S., according to the company. The amount of money given to these campaigns increased 50% since the year before. 

“The costs of regular things—food, rent, gas prices, obviously, particularly this year, and not just here but elsewhere in the world—have gone up, and folks are struggling in many cases to be able to afford all of that,” CEO Tim Cadogan told Fortune . “Things are more expensive, and a lot of people’s incomes have not moved up at a commensurate rate.”

This year’s growing fundraising demand for essentials is part of a larger trend that began during the pandemic, when the intersection of widespread job losses, health emergencies, and a transition to virtual community led more people to seek help online .

GoFundMe introduced the food, rent, and monthly bills tab in October 2020 in response to an increased need for necessities during the pandemic. Martin Lukk, a postdoctoral research fellow at the Data Sciences Institute at the University of Toronto, said while the company created the new category as a result of increased demand, it also was a catalyst for even more people seeking help through the platform.

“In response to an overwhelming number of campaigns for exactly these things, they invented this new category, and that…
items.t: ‘Folks are struggling in many cases’: GoFundMe’s CEO says affordability crisis is behind 40% surge in U.S. fundraisers for essentials like groceries

items.title: China commits to low-carbon electrification and help for others to improve
items.summary:
Exclusive: Countries at Cop31 are being urged to commit to deriving 35% of their energy from electricity by 2035

China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said.

Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, said: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. We can follow this direction while making the source of electricity clean. That’s the way to go forward.”

items.title: I hated life as a Neet. But now I’ve found a job, life is just as precarious | Emilija Morrison
items.summary:
The government’s plans to help young people not in education, work or training are welcome – I dearly hope they offer long-term security

  • Emilija Morrison is a University of Glasgow graduate and holds a Gold Standard NCTJ Diploma in journalism

What child dreams of being unemployed when they grow up? You can probably remember the days, aged 10, when you were asked to present to the class what you wanted to be. Imagine hearing this: “I want to be unemployed. After I graduate from university, I want to go to the jobcentre in my home town and collect my benefits every month.”

Yet that is the reality for many young people today – childhood dreams to become a teacher, a doctor, an engineer or whatever other profession thwarted not by the limits of their abilities, but the reality of the economy.

Emilija Morrison is a University of Glasgow graduate and holds a Gold Standard NCTJ Diploma in journalism

items.title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
items.summary:
It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains

Andy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory.

Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform. The Tories say they will rip up the agreements, though that stance carries the risk of alienating voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Nigel Farage
items.t: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
